events.text: The first full moon of the year sits in the mouth of the well like a lid. Under the water, on the cold stones, you lie: round, blue-green, the size of a fist. Somewhere a rooster clears its throat. Then feet, many feet, running on frozen earth, the clatter of jars on straw rings, women laughing and shoving, because whoever draws the first water of the year draws the dragon's egg, and the dragon's egg means a harvest.

choices.text: Glow, very faintly, toward the first dipper

effects.log: The first gourd dipper comes down through the moon and scoops you up with the water. Somebody gasps at the top of the well. Somebody else says it is only the moon in the dipper. It is not.

choices.text: Lie dark and still between the stones

effects.log: Three dippers come down and miss you. The fourth goes all the way to the bottom, slowly, as if whoever holds it is not in a hurry. It finds you. You let it.

choices.text: Listen to the feet, and choose

effects.log: One pair of feet runs, slows down for an old neighbour who has slipped on the ice, helps her up, and runs again. You roll toward that dipper. You have made your first choice, and it was a person.

events.text: The one who drew the first water, {npc}, drops a pinch of straw on the well so the others know the first water is taken, and carries the jar home on a straw ring, walking as carefully as if it held a lit lamp. In the dark kitchen the water goes into the big jar beside the hearth, and one dipper of it goes into the pot for the five-grain rice. The dipper comes down for you too.

choices.text: Cling to the inside of the dipper

mem.note: came up in my dipper on the first full moon

effects.log: {npc} sees a blue-green stone in the gourd, warm, which stones are not. {He} looks at it for a long breath, puts it back into the big water jar with both hands, and puts the lid on, and tells nobody, not even the rice.

choices.text: Sink to the bottom of the big jar

effects.log: You stay down among the dregs. The rice is cooked with the first water and the household says it is the sweetest rice in memory. {npc} cannot stop smiling, and does not know why.

choices.text: Lean toward the warmth of the hearth

effects.log: The jar stands by the fire all winter. You drink the warmth through the clay. Something inside the shell turns over, like a sleeper finding a better position.

events.text: That autumn the household has the best harvest anyone can remember, and the village says {npc} drew the dragon's egg. {npc} laughs it off at the well. But at night {he} kneels beside the water jar with a little oil lamp and looks into the water for a long time without saying anything.

choices.text: Rise to the surface and look back

mem.note: looked back at me from the water jar

effects.log: Whiskers, gold eyes, a face the size of a thumbnail. {npc} puts a hand over {his} own mouth so as not to wake the house. Neither of you blinks first.

choices.text: Stay under. Let it be a rumour

effects.log: {npc} sees only the lamp in the water and goes to bed. Rumours, you are learning, are a kind of shelter.

choices.text: Blow one bubble, exactly under the lamp

effects.log: One bubble comes up and pops. {npc} laughs out loud, then hushes, then laughs again into {his} sleeve. It is the beginning of a long conversation without words.

events.text: Every first full moon since, {npc} has run to the well before cockcrow, floated the straw, and poured the first dipper into your jar: "For the one who came home with me." This year {he} is slower on the ice, and a young neighbour with long legs is going to beat {him} to the well.

choices.text: Make the young one's dipper come up empty

effects.log: The dipper comes up with nothing in it, three times. The young neighbour stares into the well, spooked, and {npc} draws first after all. It is a small thing to do. You enjoy it a little too much.

choices.text: Let the young one win: the well is everyone's

effects.log: {npc} comes home second, out of breath, and pours the second water into your jar with exactly the same words. You understand something then: it was never about being first.

choices.text: Slip out to the well in the night and wait in it

effects.log: When {npc} lowers the dipper, the thing in it is you. {He} carries you home again through the dark, laughing so hard {he} has to stop twice.

events.text: You are as long as an ox now, and you live where the river bends below the village. One first full moon, before cockcrow, {npc} comes down the bank on a stick, very old, with a gourd dipper of well water held in both hands. "I was first one more time," {he} says to the river. "Nobody else gets up this early any more."

choices.text: Rise out of the river and drink from the dipper

effects.npcPass: old age, in the first spring after the full moon

mem.note: drank the first water from my hands

effects.log: You put your great head down to the gourd and drink. {npc} does not flinch at the size of you. "There," {he} says. "Now we are even." That spring {he} dies in {his} sleep, and the family floats straw on the well for {him}.

choices.text: Coil the length of the bank so {npc} can sit on you

effects.npcPass: old age, in the first spring after the full moon
effects.log: {npc} sits on your back in the cold like an old person on a warm wall, and talks about the year you came out of the well, until the sun comes up. It is the last time.

choices.text: Follow {him} home and lie in the old jar one more night

effects.npcPass: old age, in the first spring after the full moon
effects.log: You do not fit in the jar. You lie around it, around the kitchen, around the house, and the whole village sees the morning mist shaped like a dragon on that roof. {npc} dies that spring, smiling about it.

events.text: The youngest child of the house dips the gourd into the water jar for a drink and comes up with a green lizard with whiskers, gold eyes and three claws on each foot. The scream brings the whole household into the kitchen with lamps, the dog barking, somebody holding a broom upside down.
events.arc: The Thing in the Water Jar

choices.text: Freeze and be a lizard

ok.log: You are a lizard. A very ordinary lizard. The father of the house says lizards come in for the cool, and tips you back into the jar to be dealt with tomorrow. Tomorrow never comes.

fail.log: Lizards do not have whiskers. Everybody notices at once. The broom comes down, slowly.

choices.text: Lift your whiskers and look at them all

effects.log: Nobody screams the second time. Six people and a dog look at you in lamplight, and you look back, and something in the kitchen changes for good.

choices.text: Drop back in and stir the water dark

effects.log: The water goes cloudy as if somebody had dropped ink in. When it clears there is nothing in the jar but water. The child gets a slap for lying, and you feel bad about it for a week.

events.text: The grandmother of the house, {npc}, sends everyone out of the kitchen, lifts the lid of the jar and looks at you for a long time. Then {he} says, to the whole house through the paper door: "Nobody tells. A guest that comes in with the first water is this house's luck, and luck that is talked about walks out of the gate." From then on there is a bowl of clear water on the jar platform every dawn, and {npc} bows to it.
events.arc: The Thing in the Water Jar

choices.text: Bow your small head back to {npc}

mem.note: bowed back to me

effects.log: {npc} sees it. {He} says nothing at all, and the next morning there is a crumb of rice cake beside the water bowl.

choices.text: Hide from {him}: old people see too much

effects.log: {npc} does not mind. "Hide, then," {he} says to the jar. "That is wise. I hid for years in this house and nobody ever found me either."

choices.text: Climb out onto {his} sleeve

mem.note: climbed onto my sleeve

effects.log: You are cold and light as a wet leaf. {npc} holds very still and lets you sit on {his} wrist like a bracelet, and for a moment {he} is a girl again, and nobody is watching.

events.text: The middle child told. Of course the middle child told. A neighbour comes over "to borrow soy sauce" and drifts toward the kitchen. {npc} stands in front of the water jar like a gatepost and starts a very long story about {his} knees.
events.arc: The Thing in the Water Jar

choices.text: Hide in the soy sauce jar on the platform

effects.log: It is dark, salty and smells of four winters. You stay there until the neighbour leaves with soy sauce from a different jar. You smell like a kitchen for a month. (-5 health)

choices.text: Lie at the bottom of the water jar like a stick

ok.log: The neighbour peers in and sees a twig. "Hm," says the neighbour, and goes. {npc} finishes the story about {his} knees anyway, out of principle.

fail.log: The twig blinks. The neighbour goes home and tells the whole lane, and the household spends a year saying the neighbour is very imaginative.

choices.text: Let the neighbour see. Let them all see

effects.log: The neighbour drops the soy sauce bowl. By evening there are people at the gate. {npc} sends them all home with a broom, and then sits down by the jar, tired, and says, "You could have helped."

events.text: {npc} is dying in the warm room, and asks the family to carry the water jar to the threshold where {he} can see it. They do, all of them, without asking why. "I named you, you know," {npc} says to the jar. "In my head. Little Blue. Do not tell anyone. A dragon should have a better name."
events.arc: The Thing in the Water Jar

choices.text: Climb out and lie on the threshold beside {him}

effects.npcPass: old age, in the warm room, with the water jar at the door

mem.note: lay beside me at the end

effects.log: The family sees it, all of them, and from that night none of them ever tells. You lie beside {npc} until the breathing stops, and for a long time after.

choices.text: Stay in the jar and let {him} hear the water move

effects.npcPass: old age, in the warm room, with the water jar at the door
effects.log: You swim slow circles so the water talks against the clay all night. {npc} falls asleep listening to it and does not wake. It is the gentlest sound you know how to make.

choices.text: Breathe a little spring into the cold room

ok.npcPass: old age, in the warm room, with the water jar at the door
ok.log: The branch of dried plum in the corner puts out three blossoms in the middle of winter. {npc} sees them, says "Ah," and that is the last word. The family keeps the branch for a hundred years.

fail.npcPass: old age, in the warm room, with the water jar at the door
fail.log: Nothing comes. You are too small yet for spring. {npc} pats the jar anyway. "Next time," {he} says, and then there is no next time. (-6 health)

events.text: The house has a yellow kitchen cat called Nabi who believes, rightly, that anything that moves in the kitchen is hers. She has found the water jar. She sits on its rim with her tail around her feet and lowers one paw into the water, slowly, like a fisherman lowering a line.

choices.text: Bite the paw

effects.log: Nabi screams, you are flung against the clay, and the cat sulks on the roof for two days. You have a scratch across your nose and a reputation. (-5 health)

choices.text: Splash her in the face

effects.log: A wet cat is the most offended creature under heaven. Nabi stalks off with her ears flat. She will be back. Cats are always back.

choices.text: Hold still under the shadow of the lid

ok.log: The paw passes over you twice and finds nothing. Nabi decides the jar is boring. Being boring, you are learning, is a powerful art.

fail.log: One claw hooks your tail and drags you halfway up the jar before you twist free. (-8 health)

events.text: Night. A rat snake as long as a broom comes over the kitchen sill after the hens' eggs, and Nabi meets it in the middle of the floor with her back up. The snake is winning. You can see it from the rim of the jar.

choices.text: Drop onto the snake's head from the jar

ok.log: You land on its eyes, three claws in, and the snake forgets the cat entirely. Nabi does not forget the snake. Afterwards she sits beside the jar washing her face, as if she had done it alone. You both know.

fail.log: The snake throws you against the hearth, but it has to turn to do it, and Nabi takes it by the neck. In the morning the cat and the dragonet are both limping, and both very pleased. (-10 health)

choices.text: Thrash in the jar until the house wakes

effects.log: The jar rings like a bell. The father of the house comes in with a lamp and a hoe. Nabi gets the credit, and a fish, and that night she sleeps on the jar lid for the first time.

choices.text: Do not act. This is between a cat and a snake

effects.log: Nabi wins, barely, and limps for a season. She never sits on your jar again. You were right, perhaps. It does not feel like it.

events.text: Nabi is old now, thin as a wicker basket, and every winter night she sleeps on the lid of your water jar where the warmth of the hearth gathers. This winter she does not get down in the morning.

choices.text: Breathe warmth up through the lid

effects.log: She goes in her sleep, warm, on the lid of the jar. The child who found you buries her under the persimmon tree, and you lie still in the water all that day.

choices.text: Climb out and curl against her

effects.log: A cat and a dragon curled together on a jar lid in the first light. She purrs once. It is the only time anyone has ever purred at you.

events.text: No rain since the barley was sown. The paddies crack into tiles. The magistrate has ordered the rain rite, and now boys in blue robes go along the stone walls of the fields with gourds and jars, catching lizards, because lizards are the dragon's little kin and the dragon will not let its kin suffer.

choices.text: Watch them from the dark of the jar

effects.log: They are not cruel boys. They are hot and thirsty and doing what the old men told them. That is somehow worse.

choices.text: Slip out at dusk and warn the lizards on the wall

ok.log: Lizards do not listen to anyone, but they listen to you. Half the wall is empty in the morning. The boys catch half as many and think it is the heat.

fail.log: The lizards look at you as if you were a large, worrying lizard, and stay exactly where they are.

choices.text: Look up at the white sky and wonder why it does not rain

effects.log: You do not know yet that the sky can be asked. Some small part of you starts asking anyway.

events.text: The rite, in the yard of the district office: a row of jars, a row of boys in blue, willow sticks. They beat the jars and chant together, the old words: lizard, lizard, raise the clouds, breathe out mist, let the rain pour down and we will let you go. Inside the jars, your kin scrabble at the clay.

choices.text: Creep in at night and tip the jars over

ok.log: Three jars tip and roll. Lizards pour across the yard and over the wall like spilled beans. In the morning the clerk says the dragon must have come for its kin, and nobody argues.

fail.log: One jar rocks and settles. A dog in the yard finds you before you find the second. You get home with tooth marks. (-8 health)

choices.text: Stay and listen to the chant

effects.log: They are asking for you. Not for you, exactly, but for something like you. You learn, there in the dust, what it is to be called.

choices.text: Go home. You are too small for this

effects.log: You go home to the cool jar. The beating goes on for three days. You hear every stroke.

events.text: Out by the stream one evening, a boy in a blue robe moves faster than a boy should, and a gourd comes down over you. "A big one!" he crows. "With whiskers!" And you are in a jar, in the dark, with eleven frightened lizards.

choices.text: Bite the hand that reaches in

effects.log: He yelps and slams the lid on. You are still in the jar. But he does not put his hand in again, and the lizards press close to you, as if you were the one who knew what to do.

choices.text: Go limp, like something already dead

effects.log: He tips the jar to look, decides you are dead and keeps you anyway, because a dead lizard with whiskers is still the best thing he has ever caught.

choices.text: Look the boy in the eye

effects.log: He looks back for a long moment, uneasy. "It looked at me," he tells the others. They laugh. He does not, and he holds his stick a little more gently after that.

events.text: Bang. Bang. Bang. The sticks on the clay are like thunder from inside. Raise the clouds, breathe out mist. The lizards around you have stopped moving. It is the third day, and the sky outside is as white as paper.

choices.text: Call to the sky with everything in you

ok.log: Something in your chest goes up like a thread and catches on the sky. By noon there is a cloud. By evening, rain: thin, an hour long, enough. The boys whoop and tip every jar out in the wet. Maybe it was going to rain anyway. You will never be sure. (-10 health)

fail.log: You call until the world goes grey at the edges. The sky does not hear. On the fourth day the boys get bored and let everything go in the ditch, and you crawl home half dead. (-15 health)

choices.text: Wait for the boy who does not hit hard

effects.log: One of them only pretends to beat his jar. At night, when the others sleep, he lifts the lid and lets you all out into the ditch, whispering sorry, sorry. You remember that face.

choices.text: Climb the lizards and push the lid when the sticks stop

ok.log: The lid shifts. Twelve lizards go over the wall, and one of them has whiskers.

fail.log: The lid comes down on your claws. You get out in the end, by night, when the jar is knocked over. (-8 health)

events.text: Another dry year. A young farmer, {npc}, comes down to the stream alone, kneels, and lets a lizard out of a jar into the water. "When I was a boy we beat the jars," {he} says to nobody, or to the stream. "I caught one with whiskers once. I have felt bad about it for twelve years."

choices.text: Show {him} the whiskers

mem.note: showed itself to me, after the jars

effects.log: You come up out of the stream, much bigger than you were. {npc} sits back hard on the bank, then laughs, then bows so low {his} forehead is wet. That autumn {he} carves a little lizard on the post of {his} gate.

choices.text: Let the stream answer: a ripple, no more

effects.log: The water turns once around {his} hand, cool, and goes on. {npc} takes it as an answer. It is one.

choices.text: Stay hidden. {He} was a child

effects.log: {npc} waits until dusk and goes home. You do not need {him} to be sorry. But you find you are glad {he} was.

events.text: A dry summer again, and the boys in blue robes are out on the field walls with their jars. They are new boys. The chant is the same.

choices.text: Go among the walls before them and send the lizards home

effects.log: They catch nothing all morning and go home complaining about the heat. The old men say the dragon is sulking. The dragon is busy.

choices.text: Let one boy see you, and watch him drop the gourd

effects.log: He runs home and the rite is cancelled for a day while the elders argue about what he saw. The lizards are let go in the confusion.

choices.text: Let it run its course

effects.log: Three days of sticks on clay, and then rain, which was coming anyway. The boys let everything go. Some rites are mostly for the people who perform them.

events.text: Midnight. A spark from the kitchen hearth has jumped into the bundles of rice straw stacked for the morning fire. It is small, then not small. The family sleeps on the other side of the paper door. Every scale on your body wants to do something, and an older voice in your blood says: hidden dragon. Do not act.

choices.text: Do not act

effects.log: The dog wakes the house. They put the fire out with water from your jar, and you go out with the water, onto the hot floor, and lie in the steam unseen while they shout. Nobody knows. The voice in your blood was right. You hate it a little.

choices.text: Thrash until the jar rings like a bell

effects.log: The jar booms. The father of the house is through the door before he is awake. The fire is out in moments. In the morning they tap the jar and look at each other, and nobody says anything, carefully.

choices.text: Climb out and spit water at the flames

ok.log: A thin, hard jet, again and again, until the straw is black and wet. You are on the floor, empty, gasping, when the lamp comes. A child sees you in the steam. A child always does.

fail.log: You are too small. The heat curls your whiskers and drives you back into the jar. The dog wakes them in time. (-12 health)

events.text: A travelling scholar stays a night in the guest room and reads aloud to himself, too late, from the Book of Changes. Through the wall and the water you hear it: the first line of the first hexagram. Hidden dragon. Do not act. And then the second: the dragon is seen in the field; it is good to meet the great person.

choices.text: Hold the first line in your mouth like a stone

effects.log: Do not act. It is not the same as doing nothing. It is waiting with your whole body for the right day. You begin to see the difference.

choices.text: Hold the second line instead: the field, the great person

effects.log: Somewhere out there is a field, and in it is someone worth meeting. You fall asleep thinking about it. You dream of rice.

choices.text: Wonder who wrote a book about you

effects.log: Nobody wrote it about you. You decide to believe they did. It is the first small vanity of a long life.

events.text: A thief comes over the wall on a moonless night, a thin desperate shape, and lifts the lid of the rice chest in the store room. You can see from the jar that the rice chest is all this house has until the barley.

choices.text: Do not act. Watch who the thief is

effects.log: It is the widow from the end of the lane, who has three children and no rice. She takes one bowl, only one, and puts the lid back. In the morning the grandmother notices, and says nothing, and leaves the store room unbarred from then on.

choices.text: Knock the dipper off the jar

effects.log: Clatter. The thief is gone over the wall with nothing. In the morning the household counts the rice and is glad. You find out later who it was, and are not glad.

choices.text: Show your eyes in the dark

effects.log: Two gold eyes in the kitchen. The thief drops everything and runs, and tells the whole lane there is a goblin in that house. Nobody steals from it again for years.

events.text: A crow comes to the jar platform every morning and lays out its treasures on a lid in a row: a brass spoon, a glass bead, half a jade button. It counts them by tapping each one. Today it has seen something that shines blue-green at the bottom of the water jar: the first scale you ever shed.

choices.text: Give it the scale

effects.log: The crow takes it, lays it at the end of the row and taps it seven times, more than anything else. From then on it sits on your jar every morning as if guarding its investment.

choices.text: Keep it. It is yours

effects.log: The crow tries the lid every day for a month, then goes away to think about it. Crows are good at thinking about things.

choices.text: Trade: the scale for the glass bead

effects.log: A long negotiation, conducted entirely in stares. In the end the bead goes in your jar and the scale goes on the lid. Neither of you is sure who won, which is how a fair trade feels.

events.text: The first full moon again. The household puts a dish of sweet glutinous rice on the roof for the crows, as the old people say a crow once warned a Silla king of a plot and has been owed rice ever since. Your crow eats first, then flies down to your jar with its beak full of sticky rice, and drops it in.

choices.text: Eat it. A gift is a gift

effects.log: It is sweet, full of chestnuts and jujubes, and it clouds your water for a day. The crow watches you eat with the satisfaction of a host.

choices.text: Push it back up on to the lid

effects.log: The crow looks at the rice, then at you, then eats it itself, and comes back the next year with a dead mouse, which is worse.

choices.text: Ask the crow, in the way animals ask, what it has seen

ok.log: The crow tells you about a man on the river road with gourds on his belt who looks into every well. Crows notice who looks into wells.

fail.log: The crow tells you a great deal about another crow. You do not follow most of it.

events.text: The crow is old and its feathers have gone dull. It leads you, hopping and resting, to the hollow of a lightning pine on the hill, where it keeps everything it ever counted: spoons, buttons, a silver hairpin, a cracked mirror, and on top, still bright, your scale. It sits down on the pile and looks at you.

choices.text: Guard the hoard after it is gone

effects.log: The crow dies on the pile that winter. You leave it all there, a dragon's first hoard, and nobody ever finds that pine. Some things should just be kept.

choices.text: Give the hairpin back to the girl who lost it

effects.log: The girl from the miller's house finds her silver hairpin on her doorstep, wet, three years after it vanished. She tells everyone, and everyone looks at the sky.

choices.text: Take back your scale

effects.log: You take it gently. The crow does not object. It is time for it to stop counting.

events.text: A spring night, and the east wind comes down through the kitchen chimney like a hand reaching for you. You climb it: out of the jar, over the wall, along the irrigation ditch, into the flooded paddies under the moon, where every square of water holds its own sky.

choices.text: Follow the water channel as far as it goes

effects.log: Paddy after paddy, ditch after ditch, to the river and back by dawn. The world is green and enormous and full of frogs. You come home to the jar only to sleep, and not for long.

choices.text: Lie in the nearest paddy and look up

effects.log: Mud under your belly, sky in the water, stars in the sky. You lie there until the frogs stop singing. You do not quite go back to the jar after that night.

choices.text: Go back to the jar before dawn, but remember the way

effects.log: You are back before the household wakes. But the way out is in you now, like a path in the snow, and you take it again the next night, and the next.

events.text: The channel between the upper paddies belongs to an eel: thick as your body, longer, black and slick, and it lives in a hole in the dyke and comes out at night to tell everyone so.

choices.text: Wrestle it in the mud

ok.log: A whole night of mud and slime and knots. At dawn the eel goes downstream, insulted, and the channel is yours.

fail.log: An eel is a muscle with a mouth. It ties you in a knot and leaves you in a ditch. (-8 health)

choices.text: Share the channel: night is long enough for two

effects.log: It hunts the first half of the night, you the second. Neither of you ever agrees to this. It works for years.

choices.text: Find a different channel. There are hundreds

effects.log: The lower channel is shallower and full of loaches. You grow fat and lazy, and do not miss the eel at all.

events.text: A grey heron works the paddies at dawn, one slow step at a time, and you are exactly the size of the thing a heron wants for breakfast. The shadow of its beak falls across you.

choices.text: Freeze among the seedlings

ok.log: The beak comes down beside you and takes a frog. Stillness, again, is armour.

fail.log: The beak takes you by the tail and lifts you clean out of the water. You twist, bite, fall, and are in the deep ditch before it can stab again. (-10 health)

choices.text: Rear up and show your whiskers

effects.log: The heron has never seen a breakfast with whiskers. It considers you, decides against it, and flies off to the next valley, complaining.

choices.text: Dive into the mud of the dyke

effects.log: You learn that mud is a door, and that a heron cannot follow you through it.

events.text: Transplanting day. The whole village is in the paddies in a long row, bent double, pushing seedlings into the mud in time to the farmers' music on the dyke: gong, drum, the hourglass drum, a man singing the lead and the row answering. A bare foot comes down out of the sky, straight onto your back.

choices.text: Stay flat and take it

effects.log: The foot presses you into the mud and moves on. Its owner thinks you are a stone. You have been stepped on by the whole village, one foot at a time, and nobody knows. (-6 health)

choices.text: Slide out from under, fast

ok.log: You are three rows over before the foot lands. The music never misses a beat.

fail.log: The foot comes down on your tail. Its owner yells and falls over in the mud, and the whole row laughs, and the drummer plays something rude. Nobody believes what he says he stepped on.

choices.text: Swim along under the row, in time to the drum

effects.log: You weave through the forest of legs all afternoon to the beat of the gong. The seedlings you pass stand up straighter than the others. Next autumn the farmers argue about why.

events.text: You are as long as a dog now, and on a hot afternoon you fall asleep on the dyke in full sun, blue-green on the green, like a fallen branch of something precious. A small child comes along the dyke with a basket of greens.

choices.text: Wake, and let the child look

effects.log: The child looks at you for a long time, then puts down a bunch of shepherd's purse beside your head as an offering, and goes home and tells everyone. Nobody believes it, and everybody comes to look.

choices.text: Slide into the water without a ripple

effects.log: The child sees only the water close. But there is a dragon-shaped place in the flattened grass, and the old people come to look at it, and nod.

choices.text: Keep sleeping. What can a child do?

effects.log: The child pokes you with a stick, once, and runs. You sleep until evening. The paddy is called the Dragon Paddy from then on, though you were only in it for an afternoon.

events.text: Dusk, the stony paddy at the top of the valley that the landlord gives to whoever is too poor to argue. The tenant who works it, {npc}, straightens up from the weeds and sees you: a blue-green thing the size of a dog, with whiskers, lying in the water and looking back. {npc} does not shout. {He} takes off {his} straw hat, bows, puts the hat back on, and goes home, and tells nobody.

choices.text: Look back at {him} until {he} is gone

mem.note: looked at me in the paddy and let me go

effects.log: It is good to meet the great person, the old book says. It does not say which one is great. You watch {npc} all the way up the path to the hut, and you think: that one.

choices.text: Slip away. Being seen is new

effects.log: You are gone before {his} hat is back on. But the next evening you are in the stony paddy again, and so is {npc}, weeding very slowly near your end of it.

choices.text: Splash {his} feet as {he} passes

mem.note: splashed my feet

effects.log: {npc} stops dead, wet to the knee, and then, for the first time in what is plainly a long time, laughs.

events.text: The stony paddy gives {npc} half what any other paddy gives. Still, every evening {he} leaves a rice ball wrapped in a leaf on the dyke at your end, and sits a while, and says nothing at all, which is the most comfortable thing anyone has ever said to you.

choices.text: Breathe spring into {his} stones

mem.note: made my paddy grow

effects.log: It costs you something you did not know you had. That autumn the stony paddy is the best in the valley, and the landlord raises the rent, and {npc} pays it laughing.

choices.text: Eat the rice ball and lie beside {him} in the dusk

mem.note: kept me company at dusk

effects.log: A farmer and a dragon on a dyke, watching the light go. You learn the names of all {his} neighbours, and which ones to trust.

choices.text: Drive the fat loaches into {his} paddy

effects.log: The family eats loach soup three times that summer. {npc} knows exactly who to thank and thanks the water, carefully, every time.

events.text: The landlord's steward comes up the valley with two men and a list. {npc} is behind on the rent, and the stony paddy is to go to someone who will pay more for it now that it grows. The steward stands on your dyke and reads the list out loud. {npc} stands in the water with {his} head down.

choices.text: Do not act. This is a human matter

effects.log: You lie still. {npc} begs, bargains and in the end borrows the rent from three neighbours at a terrible rate. {He} keeps the paddy. It takes {him} six years to pay it back. You watch every one of them.

choices.text: Let the dyke give way under the steward

ok.log: The dyke slumps and the steward sits down in the paddy up to the chest, list and all, and leaves with mud in the hat, saying the paddy is cursed. Nobody else wants it. {npc} keeps it for the old rent.

fail.log: The dyke holds. You strain against it until something in your back twinges. The steward finishes reading and goes. (-6 health)

choices.text: Rise out of the water behind the steward

effects.log: The two men see you first. The steward turns around last, and does not finish the list. The rent on the stony paddy is never raised again, and the steward tells the landlord a story nobody believes, except the landlord, at night.

events.text: A hungry spring. The barley is not ripe and the rice is gone, and the family on the stony paddy eats pine bark and boiled grass. {npc} comes down to the dyke in the evening as always, and sits as always, and does not ask you for anything. That is what makes it hard.

choices.text: Shed a scale for {him} to sell

mem.note: gave me a scale in the hungry spring

effects.log: It hurts like pulling a tooth. A blue-green scale, the size of a palm, on the dyke. {npc} looks at it for a long time, then takes it to the apothecary in town, who pays in rice and asks no questions, and asks them later of everyone else. (-8 health)

choices.text: Lead the fish of the whole river into {his} paddy

ok.log: For a week {his} paddy boils with carp. {npc} feeds the family and then the lane and then half the village, and does not say where the fish came from.

fail.log: The fish do not understand what you want. A few loaches, a frog. {npc} thanks you anyway, and the family gets through the spring on pine bark and stubbornness.

choices.text: Lie beside {him}: some springs are only to be endured

effects.log: You do not fix it. You stay. The family lives through it, thinner. Afterwards {npc} says it helped to have you there, and you are not sure whether {he} means it.

events.text: {npc} has grey in {his} topknot now, and brings a grandchild down to the dyke on {his} back. "Bow," {he} tells the child, and the child bows to the paddy, puzzled. "Why?" "Because it is polite to bow to the people who have been good to you," {npc} says, "even if they are in the water."

choices.text: Show yourself to the grandchild

mem.note: showed itself to my grandchild

effects.log: The child does not cry. The child reaches for your whiskers, and you let it. The story goes into that family that day, and it does not come out again for three hundred years.

choices.text: Stay under, and let it be the grandfather's story

effects.log: The child sees nothing and bows anyway. Years later the grandchild tells it to their own children: grandfather bowed to the water, and the water bowed back.

choices.text: Send a ripple up the paddy, like a bow

effects.log: The whole paddy shivers from end to end. The child shrieks with joy. {npc} only nods, as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world.

events.text: The funeral bier comes down the valley road, bright with paper flowers, the bearers singing the old dirge, the bell-ringer calling the lines. It is {npc}. As it passes the stony paddy the bearers stop, though nobody told them to, and turn the bier toward the water.

choices.text: Rise in full sight and bow to the bier

effects.npcPass: old age, in the house by the stony paddy
effects.log: The bearers see you. The mourners see you. The whole valley sees an ox-long dragon rise out of a poor paddy and bow its horned head to a tenant farmer. They will tell it for centuries, and they will always get the farmer's name right.

choices.text: Bring rain, just on the road, just for the bier

ok.npcPass: old age, in the house by the stony paddy
ok.log: A grey cloud the size of a threshing floor stands over the road and rains on the bier all the way to the hill, and nowhere else. The family says heaven wept. You know who wept.

fail.npcPass: old age, in the house by the stony paddy
fail.log: The sky does not come. You strain until your horn buds ache, and the bier goes on up the hill in the dry, and you lie in the paddy afterwards, emptied. (-10 health)

choices.text: Follow under the water of the ditches, unseen, to the hill

effects.npcPass: old age, in the house by the stony paddy
effects.log: You go with {npc} the whole way, through every ditch and channel, the last walk you take together. Nobody sees you. That is how {he} would have wanted it.

events.text: The day the old almanac calls the waking of the insects. All along the dykes the frogs come up out of the mud, blinking, and start to sing, and something in you that has been asleep without your knowing comes up with them.

choices.text: Sing with the frogs, in your way

effects.log: Your way is a low hum in the water that makes the frogs fall silent, then sing louder. The village says it is the loudest spring in years.

choices.text: Lie still and feel what is waking

effects.log: It is not in your body. It is in the ground under you, all the way to the mountains. You are, somehow, part of the spring. You do not know yet that you are the spring.

events.text: The spring equinox: day and night exactly level, the scales of the year balanced. At dawn an urge seizes you like hunger: to go up. Out of the water, into the air, toward the east, where seven stars you cannot see yet are waiting in daylight.

choices.text: Rise: leap as high as you can

effects.log: You leap clear of the paddy, higher than a man, and hang for a breath in the east wind, and fall back with a slap that empties the dyke. Somebody on the road sees a green flash. It was the best moment of your life so far.

choices.text: Feel the urge, and do not answer it yet

effects.log: You hold it in your chest all day, like a breath. Hidden dragon. The urge passes at dusk and leaves something behind: the knowledge that you could.

events.text: The autumn equinox, and the other urge: down. The paddies are drained and golden, the threshing has begun, and something pulls you toward the deepest, darkest water you know, as if the year wanted you to put it away.

choices.text: Dive to the bottom of the river pool and stay there

effects.log: You lie in the dark under the bend for a whole month and come up lighter, as if you had left something heavy at the bottom. The old book was right: a dragon rises in spring and dives in autumn.

choices.text: Refuse it. Stay up and watch the threshing

effects.log: You watch the flails go up and down on the threshing floor until the first frost. You feel very awake, and slightly wrong, like a bird that did not fly south.

events.text: Midwinter, the longest night. The household boils red bean porridge and flicks it on the gate posts and the walls to keep the spirits off, and a spoonful lands in your ditch, red on the ice.

choices.text: Eat it

effects.log: It is hot and sweet and has rice cake balls in it. Whatever it is supposed to keep away, it does not keep you away. You decide you are not a spirit. Probably.

choices.text: Stay off the gate that night, out of courtesy

effects.log: You spend the longest night under the ice in the far paddy. In the morning the porridge on the gate is untouched by anything, and the household is pleased with how well it worked.

events.text: You have lived enough years now to count them by your own body: the rise in spring, the dive in autumn, in and out, like breathing. One equinox morning you notice that the valley is breathing with you.

choices.text: Breathe slower, and see if the valley follows

effects.log: The plum blossoms open a day late. Then two. You stop at once, frightened and thrilled. Something this large should not be in the hands of something this small.

choices.text: Breathe exactly with the year, never ahead of it

effects.log: You fall into step with the seasons like a farmer falls into step with the drum. It is not power. It is something better than power, and harder to lose.

events.text: A fox with two tails sits on the paddy dyke in the moonlight, washing its face. "Little dragon," it says, pleasantly. "Your egg-shell. Someone in the house buried the pieces under the jar platform. A dragon's shell keeps its warmth for a hundred years, and a fox's third tail is a cold thing to grow. I would like it."

choices.text: Give it the shell

effects.log: You dig it up yourself and bring it, piece by piece. The fox takes each piece in its teeth as delicately as an egg. "Generous," it says. "Foolish. I will remember both."

choices.text: Refuse. It is yours

effects.log: "Of course," says the fox, still pleasant, and goes. You do not believe for a moment that it has given up. Neither does it.

choices.text: Ask what it will give you

effects.log: "A fox's answer to any one question," it says. You ask what you are. It laughs for a long time. "The east," it says at last, "but small yet." You give it the shell. It was a fair price.

events.text: The fox is back, with a bead of light in its mouth like a drop of the moon. It rolls the bead from cheek to cheek. "A fox bead," it says around it. "Hold it in your mouth for one night and you will know what foxes know. Then give it back. Do give it back."

choices.text: Take the bead for one night, and give it back

effects.log: One night of knowing what foxes know: where every grave is, who lies, what the dead want. In the morning you give it back, and the fox looks surprised, and then, for the first time, respectful.

choices.text: Swallow it

ok.log: The bead goes down like cold fire. The fox screams like a woman and runs, and for a year you understand things you have no right to. The fox does not forgive you. Foxes do not.

fail.log: It is not meant for a dragon. You are sick for a season, and cough it up in the end, black, and the fox takes it and is gone without a word. (-15 health)

choices.text: Refuse. Nothing a fox offers is free

effects.log: "Wise," says the fox, with its mouth full of moon. "Boring, but wise."

events.text: A child of the village has been going out at night to the old graves on the hill, sleepwalking, and coming back pale. You know a fox's work when you see it. Up on the hill, under the moon, something with a red tail is digging.

choices.text: Go up the hill and stand between the fox and the child

ok.log: The fox looks at you a long time over the open grave. "Small yet," it says, "but east." It goes. The child sleeps through the night after that.

fail.log: The fox is older than the village. It bites you to the bone and leaves you in the grave. But it leaves the child too, and does not come back. (-12 health)

choices.text: Wake the child's household by rattling every jar on their platform

effects.log: The household wakes, finds the child gone, and runs up the hill with torches and gongs. The fox does not like gongs. Nobody does.

choices.text: Do not act. Foxes and graves are not your business

effects.log: The child is ill all winter, and the exorcist the family hires is expensive and useless. In spring the fox moves on. You tell yourself it worked out.

events.text: A fox with three tails comes down to the river at dusk, and the third tail is the warmest red you have ever seen. "Your shell," it says, or "your bead," depending on what you did. "I said I would remember. Foxes pay their debts too, one way or the other."

choices.text: Ask it to pay in warning

effects.log: "Men with iron," it says. "Not yet. Not for a long time. But they will come for the veins of this land, and they will come at night." It goes. You do not understand it for a hundred years.

choices.text: Ask it to leave the village children alone, for ever

effects.log: "For ever is long for a fox," it says. "But yes." It keeps its word. The village never knows how lucky it is.

choices.text: Tell it there is no debt

effects.log: The fox looks at you as if you had said something very strange in a language it almost knows. Then it bows, three tails low, and goes into the reeds.

events.text: Winter. You are asleep at the bottom of the old water jar when the household buys a new one from a jar peddler with a tower of pots roped to the wooden frame on his back, and sells him the old one, cracked lip and all, for a handful of coins. Nobody looks inside. The world tips over, and you are on the road.

choices.text: Stay asleep. It is winter

effects.log: You wake three valleys away, swaying, roped between a soy sauce pot and a kimchi jar, the peddler humming the same four notes over and over.

choices.text: Wake, but stay curious

effects.log: You watch the road unroll through a crack in the lid: frozen rivers, an inn, a stone guardian post with a wide grin. You have never seen so much world.

choices.text: Rattle the jar to be heard

ok.log: The peddler stops, puts the frame down, peers into the jar, and sees nothing, because you have changed your mind. He shrugs and walks on. At least now you know he is the kind who looks.

fail.log: He only tightens the rope, which tilts you on your head for the rest of the day. (-5 health)

events.text: Market day in a river town, the five-day market, salt and dried fish and straw shoes and noise. Your jar stands in a row of jars on a mat. A rich house's cook taps each jar with a knuckle, listening for cracks, and stops at yours, because yours taps back.

choices.text: Tap again

effects.log: The cook takes the lid off, sees you, puts the lid back on, pays double and carries the jar to the river and empties it in the shallows. "I did not see that," the cook says to the river, and goes home with an empty jar and a story.

choices.text: Wait until night and climb out into the river

effects.log: The market packs up. In the dark you go over the rim, over the mat, down the bank and into cold black water that smells of somewhere else.

choices.text: Make yourself small and dull and sold

effects.log: You are sold for soy sauce. The cook's house is three streets from the river. That night you leave by the drain, which is a dignity you will not mention to anyone.

events.text: The long way home: up a river you do not know, against the current, in the cold, with nothing to steer by but the taste of the water. Somewhere upstream, very faint, is the taste of one well.

choices.text: Follow the taste, however long it takes

effects.log: Twenty days, a weir, a mill race, a waterfall you have to climb twice. You come up out of the ditch behind your old house on the first night of spring and lie in the new water jar as if you had never left. The household pretends not to notice. They are very relieved.

choices.text: Stay a season in the river town first

effects.log: You learn a town: the ferry, the market, the governor's pond with its fat carp. Then you go home, changed, carrying a town in your head.

choices.text: Let a ferry carry you part of the way, under its hull

effects.log: The ferryman wonders all week why the boat feels lighter going upstream. You let go at the right bend and swim the rest.

events.text: A wandering monk comes to the gate tapping a wooden fish, tok, tok, tok, with an alms bowl and a grey robe patched at both elbows. The household gives {him} a scoop of barley. On the way out {npc} stops by the water jar, or the ditch, wherever you are, and looks straight at you, and smiles.

choices.text: Look back

mem.note: looked back at me

effects.log: {npc} puts {his} palms together and bows, as to an equal. Then {he} goes, tok, tok, tok, down the road, and asks nothing, and tells nobody. You did not know people could do that.

choices.text: Hide

effects.log: {npc} bows to the place you were anyway. "Good," {he} says softly. "Stay hidden a while yet."

choices.text: Ask, in the way water asks, what {he} sees

effects.log: "Spring," {npc} says, as if you had spoken. "Very small. Very early. Be patient with yourself." And then {he} goes.

events.text: Some years later the same tok, tok on the road. {npc} sits down on the dyke without asking anyone, unwraps a cold rice ball, and recites a sutra to the paddy in a low voice, all the way through, as if you had asked for it. Then {he} eats the rice ball.

choices.text: Listen to the whole sutra

effects.log: You understand perhaps one word in twenty. The one that stays is the one about all things arising and passing away. You are not sure you like it. You keep it anyway.

choices.text: Steal half the rice ball

effects.log: {npc} laughs so hard {he} loses {his} place in the sutra and has to start again from the beginning, which {he} does, happily.

choices.text: Ask why {he} asks you for nothing

effects.log: "Everyone will ask you for something soon enough," {npc} says. "Rain, sons, revenge. I thought one person should not."

events.text: The last time {npc} comes down the road, {he} is very old and walks with a staff, and {he} does not tap the wooden fish. {He} lays it on the dyke beside the water. "I will not need it," {npc} says. "You might, one day, when everyone is asking you for things. Tap it and remember one person did not."

choices.text: Keep the wooden fish

effects.npcPass: old age, at a hermitage in the mountains
effects.log: You keep it under the bank. Every time, for centuries, that pride rises in you like a tide, you go and look at it. It does not do anything. It does not have to.

choices.text: Follow {him} to the edge of the valley

effects.npcPass: old age, at a hermitage in the mountains
effects.log: You go along the ditches beside the road as far as the water goes. At the last ditch {npc} bows, as to an equal, and goes up into the mountains, and you never hear the tok, tok again.

events.text: The summer rains come all at once, forty days of them, and on the fortieth night the river forgets its banks. The flood comes down the valley brown and roaring, full of trees and thatch and drowned pigs, and it takes the paddies, and it takes you.

choices.text: Fight the current for the bank

ok.log: You claw into a willow root and hold all night while the river tries to tear you off it. In the morning you are on the bank, alive, a long way from anything you know.

fail.log: The river is the strongest thing you have ever met. It beats you against a dam of trees until you stop fighting. (-30 health)
fail.deathCause: the summer flood, fighting the river

choices.text: Go with the water: you are a water thing

effects.log: You let it take you, and keep your head up, and ride the flood like a leaf. Three days later you wash up in a backwater by a ferry landing, bruised and astonished to be alive.

choices.text: Dive under the flood to the riverbed

ok.log: Under the roar the riverbed is almost still. You lie flat in the dark and let the flood go over you like weather. You learn that every storm has a floor.

fail.log: A rolling boulder finds you on the bottom. You come up somewhere downstream, half drowned. (-15 health)

events.text: The ferry landing at the river crossing, wrecked, the ferry boat upside down on the sand. The ferry family is out in the wreckage with poles: an old ferryman and a sharp-eyed grandchild, {npc}, who spots you in the tangle of driftwood and shouts that there is a giant eel.

choices.text: Let {him} pull you out with the pole

mem.note: pulled out of the flood wreck

effects.log: {npc} hauls, the old ferryman hauls, and out of the driftwood comes something that is not an eel. The old man sits down on the sand. {npc} does not. {npc} says: "I knew it."

choices.text: Free yourself and slip away

effects.log: You tear out of the driftwood and into the river. {npc} sees a whiskered head go under and spends the rest of the summer watching the water.

choices.text: Help them right the ferry first

ok.log: You get your back under the gunwale and heave, and the boat rolls over right side up with a boom. The old ferryman bows to the river three times. {npc} just stares, delighted.

fail.log: It is too heavy for you yet. But {npc} saw you try, and that is the beginning of something. (-8 health)

events.text: You stay at the crossing that autumn while you heal. {npc} poles the rebuilt ferry across and back all day, and talks to the water the whole way, about everything. One evening a rich merchant on the ferry, impatient, pushes {npc} aside to take the pole, and the boat turns broadside to the current.

choices.text: Put your shoulder under the hull and set it straight

mem.note: held the ferry straight

effects.log: The ferry swings back into line as if it had been pushed by a hand. The merchant falls over the bundles. {npc} takes the pole back without a word, grinning at the water.

choices.text: Let the merchant learn the river

effects.log: The boat spins twice and fetches up on a sand bar, and the merchant has to wade ashore in silk. Nobody is hurt but the silk. {npc} laughs about it for a year.

choices.text: Rise beside the boat and look at the merchant

effects.log: The merchant gives the pole back with great politeness and pays the fare three times over, and never takes that ferry again.

events.text: Time to go home, up the river. {npc} comes down to the landing at dawn with a rice ball and a little straw boat with a candle in it, and sets it on the water. "So you can find the way," {npc} says. "Come back. Ferries need someone underneath them."

choices.text: Promise, in the way water promises

mem.note: promised to come back to the crossing

effects.log: You come back every summer the river runs high. The crossing never loses a boat again in {his} lifetime. When {npc} is old, the ferry family builds a little shrine at the landing, facing the water.

choices.text: Push the candle boat ahead of you all the way up the river

effects.log: It goes out after a mile, of course. You keep pushing it anyway, all the way home, and leave it in the paddy where you were born.

choices.text: Go without looking back

effects.log: {npc} watches the water for a long time. You know, because you watch {him} from the next bend.

events.text: You have been sleeping in the corner of one paddy all summer because the mud there is cool. Where you sleep, the rice grows twice as fast as anywhere else in the valley, and the village has started coming to look at it.

choices.text: Move around: share it out

effects.log: You sleep in a different paddy every night. By autumn the whole valley has a good year and no single paddy is strange. The old people say it is a dragon year, and are right.

choices.text: Stay. It is your corner

effects.log: The corner of that paddy grows rice taller than a child. People come from the next valley to see it. The owner charges them to stand on the dyke.

choices.text: Find out whose paddy it is

effects.log: It belongs to a widow who works it alone with her daughter, the poorest paddy owners in the valley. You find that you do not want to move after all.

events.text: The village headman and a landlord's son stand on the dyke of your green paddy and talk loudly about buying it, or swapping it, or simply taking it, since the owner has no one to argue for her.

choices.text: Leave the paddy. The rice will be ordinary again

effects.log: You sleep elsewhere. The rice in that corner is ordinary the next year. The landlord's son loses interest. The owner keeps the paddy and never knows why it stopped being special, and why it is still hers.

choices.text: Stay, and make the landlord's son's paddy wither instead

effects.log: One night in his paddy, breathing out instead of in. The rice yellows from the roots. The village takes the lesson. You are not sure it was the right lesson.

choices.text: Let them see what sleeps in the corner

effects.log: You lift your head out of the rice as they argue. The headman falls off the dyke. Nobody ever talks about buying that paddy again, and the village starts calling it the Dragon's Bed.

events.text: At harvest the village has started a new custom, nobody remembers who began it: in every paddy they leave one corner uncut, a few sheaves standing, for the one who sleeps in the rice.

choices.text: Eat a little from every corner

effects.log: You go round the valley on the night of the harvest moon and take a mouthful from each corner. The next morning every corner is flattened in the same shape. The custom becomes law.

choices.text: Leave the corners for the sparrows and the poor

effects.log: The gleaners find the corners untouched and take them home. The village decides the dragon gives its share to the poor, and starts doing the same, which is how a custom becomes a kindness.

events.text: First full moon. On the hill the village burns the moon house, a tower of straw and pine, and children run about with lanterns. One paper lantern breaks loose from a child's stick and comes down into your stream, still lit, a wish brushed on its side in a child's careful hand: let my brother come home from the soldiers.

choices.text: Carry it to the bank, still burning

mem.note: brought my wish back out of the stream

effects.log: The child, {npc}, is there on the bank crying for it, and sees it come out of the water on the back of something with whiskers. {npc} stops crying at once.

choices.text: Keep the wish. Take it into the deep pool

effects.log: You lie with the paper on your back until the ink runs into the water. You do not know what a wish is for. You think you will find out.

choices.text: Blow the flame bigger as it floats away

effects.log: The lantern flares and sails down the stream like a little sun. {npc} on the bank claps both hands over {his} mouth, as if the wish had been heard.

events.text: The soldiers' road runs along your river, and that summer men come home along it from the northern border, thin and sunburnt, in twos and threes. {npc} sits on the bank every evening watching the road. One evening, at the ford, a lone soldier stops because the water is too high to cross.

choices.text: Lift the ford for the soldier: lie across it like a bridge

mem.note: brought my brother over the ford

effects.log: The soldier steps on something solid and does not look down, and crosses dry, and is at the gate before dark. {npc} runs down the lane screaming a name. The wish had a ford in it all along.

choices.text: Let the water drop, quietly

mem.note: brought my brother home

ok.log: The river sinks a hand's breadth, then two, and the soldier crosses. Brother and sibling meet on the bank. You lie low under the ford, pleased beyond words.

fail.log: The water will not listen. The soldier waits a day for it to drop by itself, and comes home a day late. Nobody minds a day.

choices.text: Do not act. If it is the brother, the road will bring the brother home

effects.log: The soldier comes the next day, by the bridge downstream. {npc} never knows the river was listening. You do.

events.text: Years later, on another first full moon, {npc} comes down to the stream grown, with a child of {his} own and a paper lantern. On it, brushed in a careful hand: for whoever lives in this stream. Thank you.

choices.text: Carry this one to the deep pool and keep it

effects.log: You keep it under the bank as long as paper lasts, which is not long, and as long as you last, which is.

choices.text: Show yourself to the child

effects.log: The child sees whiskers in the lantern light and does not scream, because {npc} has told this story at bedtime for years. "Is that it?" "That is it." The child bows exactly as {npc} taught.

choices.text: Light every lantern on the hill a little brighter

effects.log: All the lanterns flare at once. The moon-house fire roars. The whole village gasps and claps. Only {npc} looks at the stream.

events.text: A dream: another well, another village, the same first full moon, the same cold stones, and on them another egg. You wake knowing, the way you know the season, that you were not the only one the sky laid that night.

choices.text: Go looking

effects.log: You go up every stream that leaves the valley, one by one, and come back from each with nothing but a taste in your mouth that is almost familiar.

choices.text: Call, in the way water calls

effects.log: You put the call into the river and let it go. Days later, very faint, something calls back from over the ridge.

choices.text: Let it be a dream

effects.log: Some things you are not ready to know. The dream comes back every first full moon anyway.

events.text: Up at the watershed where two valleys' streams begin a stone's throw apart, you find it: another young dragon, a little bigger than you, a little darker, with a torn whisker and the eyes of someone who did not have a grandmother to keep them secret.

choices.text: Greet it as kin

effects.log: It does not know what kin is. You show it. A whole day of chasing each other through the shallows, and at dusk it goes back down its own valley looking back twice.

choices.text: Size it up: who is stronger?

ok.log: You wrestle in the snowmelt until it gives way. It is not angry. It seems to have expected it. You are not sure what you have won.

fail.log: It is stronger. It pins you in the cold water and looks at you with interest, and lets you go. (-8 health)

choices.text: Ask about its well

effects.log: The one who drew its first water threw it back down the well in terror. It hatched alone in the dark and climbed out by itself. You think of your own jar, and are quiet.

events.text: A dry summer, and your sibling has been taking the rain. Not on purpose, perhaps. But the clouds that should come over the ridge to your valley stop at its valley and empty there, and its paddies are green, and yours are not.

choices.text: Go up to the watershed and talk

ok.log: It did not know it was doing it. It is horrified, then defensive, then sorry. You agree to take turns breathing. It is the first treaty of your life.

fail.log: "The clouds come to whoever is bigger," it says. It is bigger. You go home with that in your teeth.

choices.text: Fight it for the clouds

ok.log: Two young dragons tearing up the snowmelt at the watershed. When it is over, the clouds come to your side. Your sibling does not come to the watershed again for many years.

fail.log: It is bigger. It hurts you badly and keeps the rain. (-25 health)
fail.deathCause: your own kin, at the watershed

choices.text: Let it have this summer. Rain comes round

effects.log: Your valley has a thin year. The next summer the clouds come to you, and your sibling sends them over the ridge without being asked.

events.text: Your sibling comes to the watershed one last time. It has grown restless, and it smells of salt. "I am going down to the sea," it says. "There is a Dragon King there with a palace, and nobody in my valley ever wanted me. Come."

choices.text: Stay. Your valley wanted you

effects.log: It goes alone, down to the sea. Once a century, on the first full moon, you taste salt in the river and know it is thinking of you.

choices.text: Go with it as far as the river mouth

effects.log: Nine days down the river together. At the mouth, where the water goes salt, you stop and it goes on. It does not look back. You wish it had.

choices.text: Ask it to stay, and share the ridge

ok.log: It stays, in the next valley, over the ridge. For the rest of your lives two dragons breathe on either side of one mountain, and the farmers say it is the luckiest range in the province.

fail.log: "You have a jar to go home to," it says, not unkindly. "I do not." It goes to the sea.

events.text: Dano, the fifth day of the fifth month. Girls wash their hair in iris water and fly on the swings; on the riverbank sand the village men wrestle for an ox. You watch from the reeds as a huge farmhand throws everyone who steps into the ring, until a small, clever miller's boy steps in and hooks the giant's leg by the belt.

choices.text: Watch how the small one wins

effects.log: He does not win by strength. He wins by being where the giant's weight is about to be. The giant goes down on his back in the sand, and the crowd roars, and you lie in the reeds thinking about weight for a week.

choices.text: Watch how the big one loses

effects.log: He loses because he has never had to think. You resolve, there in the reeds, always to have to think.

choices.text: Nudge the sand under the giant's heel

effects.log: The heel slides a finger's width. The miller's boy wins the ox. He will never know he had help, and you will never quite forget that he did.

events.text: The miller's boy practises alone on the riverbank at night now, throwing a sack of sand, again and again, because the giant has sworn to beat him next Dano. You are in the water a stone's throw away, and you are curious what it would be like to wrestle.

choices.text: Grab the end of the sack from the water and pull

ok.log: He pulls. You pull. He finds he is wrestling the river, and he does not let go, and he does not lose. Neither do you. At dawn he goes home stronger, and so do you.

fail.log: He yanks the sack, and you, out of the water onto the sand, and stares at what he has caught. You are back in the river before he can scream. He practises somewhere else after that. (-5 health)

choices.text: Watch his feet, every night, and learn

effects.log: Weight, balance, the hook of the leg. You have no legs to speak of, but you have a body that is all balance, and you learn more than he does.

choices.text: Leave him in peace. Strength is lonely work

effects.log: He wins the next Dano. When he is given the ox, he bows to the river, for no reason he can explain.

events.text: The giant farmhand never won the ox again, and has found other uses for his size: he collects "debts" for a moneylender up and down the valley, and nobody dares refuse him. Today he is shaking an old man by the collar on the bridge over your river.

choices.text: Hook his leg from under the bridge, the way the boy did

ok.log: Something takes his ankle and pulls, exactly the way the miller's boy did all those years ago, and the giant goes over the rail into the river. He comes up spluttering, and the old man is gone. Strength, you think, is for this.

fail.log: He is heavier than he looks, and kicks. But the old man runs while he does. (-10 health)

choices.text: Rise beside the bridge and look at him

effects.log: He lets go of the collar. He backs off the bridge. He leaves the valley that week, and the moneylender has to collect his own debts, which he is bad at.

choices.text: Do not act. The miller's boy will deal with him

effects.log: He does, the next day, in front of the whole market, with the same leg hook. The valley laughs for a month. Sometimes the person who should act is someone else.

events.text: Your well, the one you were laid in, goes dry. The women stand around it with empty jars on their heads and look down at a circle of cracked mud, and nobody says anything, because a dry well is the worst thing a village can see. You are at the bottom of it, in the mud, and you are too small to do anything at all.

choices.text: Call the rain anyway

effects.log: Nothing. Not a cloud. You lie in the mud with your head ringing, and learn the hardest lesson of the small: wanting is not enough. (-8 health)

choices.text: Dig for the spring under the mud

ok.log: You follow the cold down through the mud with your claws, and find it: a thread of water, sulking under a stone. You move the stone. By morning there is a hand's depth in the well, enough for drinking, and the women weep at the rim.

fail.log: You dig all night and find only more mud. (-5 health)

choices.text: Stay, so the well is not empty

effects.log: You lie in the bottom of the dry well all through the drought. You cannot fill it. But it is not empty. Something in that seems to matter, though you cannot say what.

events.text: The village men lower a ladder into the well to dig it deeper. A young man comes down with a mattock and a lamp, and finds you in the mud at the bottom, and freezes.

choices.text: Show him where to dig

effects.log: You put your claw on one stone and look at him. He digs there. Water. He goes up the ladder with his mouth open and never tells anyone what showed him, only that the well wanted him to dig there.

choices.text: Slip into a crack in the stones

effects.log: He decides it was the lamp. He digs where he likes, and finds water at the third try, and you are glad.

choices.text: Hiss him back up the ladder

effects.log: He goes up faster than he came down. The village decides the well has an angry spirit and calls a shaman for a well rite, which is a lot of rice cakes and drumming for one small dragon.

events.text: The rains come back at last. The village holds a rite at the well to thank its spirit: a shaman in a bright robe, a drum, rice cakes and a pig's head on a straw mat, a bowl of the first new water set on the rim. The shaman stops dancing in the middle and peers down into the well.

choices.text: Rise to meet the shaman's eyes

effects.log: The shaman sees you and does not stop the drum, which is professional of her. Afterwards she tells the village the well spirit is young and blue and should be given clean water, not pig. They give you clean water every year.

choices.text: Eat a rice cake off the mat when no one is looking

effects.log: One rice cake is missing at the end of the rite. The shaman counts them twice and declares the rite a great success.

choices.text: Stay under. The thanks belong to the rain

effects.log: You were too small to save the well. You let the thanks go up to the sky with the drumming, where it belongs.

events.text: A man comes up the river road with gourds and bamboo cages hanging all over, rattling. A minor cultivator, {npc}, collecting strange creatures for a sect's beast garden: three-legged toads, white sparrows, a fish with a face. {He} stops at your paddy. {He} looks at the water for a long time. {He} smiles.

choices.text: Ride the wind away before {he} moves

ok.log: The east wind takes you three paddies over and into the river while {npc} is still unrolling the net. {He} laughs. "Quick," {he} says to the empty water. "Good. Quick ones fetch more."

fail.log: A silk net cuts the air. You tear out of it, leaving a scale and some blood, and get away into the reeds. {npc} picks up the scale and holds it to the light for a long time. (-8 health)

choices.text: Lie still in the mud like a log

effects.log: {npc} wades in to the knees, pokes about, finds nothing, and goes. But {he} marks the paddy on a scrap of paper, and you saw {him} do it.

choices.text: Bite the first hand that reaches in

effects.log: {npc} yelps, then grins through it with blood on {his} wrist. "Teeth," {he} says. "Better and better."

events.text: {npc} has set traps. A live hen tied to a stake in your paddy at dusk. Fine silk nets across the mouths of the ditches. A bowl of something sweet and drugged on the dyke. And {npc}, somewhere in the dark, breathing very quietly, the way cultivators breathe.

choices.text: Leave everything alone and go upriver for a season

effects.log: You go. {npc} sits by the hen for a month and the hen grows fat and tame. In the end {he} eats it, and leaves, swearing.

choices.text: Free the hen and spring every net

ok.log: In the morning every net is down and the hen is in the farmer's yard. {npc} stares at the ruin of the traps, and then, despite everything, bows to the paddy.

fail.log: The third net was a double. It closes over you, and you have to cut through it with your claws while {npc} runs up the dyke. You barely make the river. (-12 health)

choices.text: Eat the sweet thing

effects.log: It is honey and something bitter. You wake at noon in the reeds a mile away, with no memory of getting there and a burst net beside you. (-10 health)

events.text: This time {npc} has a sect brother with {him} and an iron cage, and they come in daylight, from both ends of the paddy at once. There is nowhere to be a log, and nowhere to be quick.

choices.text: Fight through them

ok.log: Teeth, tail, mud, a cage rolling into the ditch. The sect brother runs. {npc} sits in the paddy holding {his} arm and laughing like someone who has finally seen the thing {he} came for.

fail.log: Iron touches you, and burns, and you learn what dragons have always known about iron. You get away only because the cage gets stuck in the mud. (-30 health)
fail.deathCause: a catcher's iron cage, before you were grown

choices.text: Ride the spring wind straight up and away

effects.log: You go up out of the paddy on a gust of east wind that flattens the rice and takes {npc}'s hat. They stand in the mud staring at the sky. You do not come back to that valley for a year.

choices.text: Go into the ditch under the village headman's house

effects.log: They cannot dig up the headman's yard without asking, and the headman, who has heard about the dragon paddy, says no. A village can be a shelter too.

events.text: {npc} comes back a decade later alone, lame, without gourds or cages. The sect threw {him} out for coming home empty-handed. {He} sits on the dyke and talks to the water. "I only want to see you once," {npc} says. "Not to take. I have spent my life catching things and I have never once just looked at one."

choices.text: Let {him} look

mem.note: let me look at it, at last

effects.log: You come out of the water and lie on the dyke in the sun, an arm's length away. {npc} looks for an hour, crying a little, and does not move {his} hands once. Then {he} goes down the road and becomes a teacher of village children, and teaches them never to cage anything.

choices.text: Stay under. Some promises are bait

effects.log: {npc} waits until dark, nods as if that were fair, and goes. You never know if {he} meant it. That is the price of being careful.

choices.text: Show yourself, then send {him} off with a warning

effects.log: A look, then the whole length of you in the water, then teeth. {npc} goes, satisfied and terrified, which may be what {he} needed.

events.text: Your claws were soft as a fingernail when you hatched. This spring the third and last on each foot goes hard, white as pearl, and itches. On the cool stone at the rim of your old well you put your foot down and pull, and a thin bright line appears in the granite.

choices.text: Leave the mark

effects.log: Three thin lines on the well stone. The women say a sickle did it. The stone will outlast the sickle, the women, and the village, and the lines will still be there.

choices.text: Smooth it over with your belly

effects.log: You rub the stone until the line is a faint scar only you could find. Hidden dragon. You are learning.

choices.text: Scratch a little more: a whisker, an eye

effects.log: Your first picture of yourself, on the well stone, a hand long. It is not very good. You are very proud of it.

events.text: Your claws are long enough now to score a boulder. On the big grey stone at the head of the paddies, where children dry their feet, there are suddenly three deep grooves that nobody made, and the children have started putting their fingers in them for luck.

choices.text: Let them believe it is luck

effects.log: It becomes luck, because they believe it. Children put their fingers in the grooves before every exam, wedding and long road for the next four hundred years.

choices.text: Add a fourth groove, just to see

effects.log: You do not have a fourth claw. The fourth groove is ragged and wrong. You will have one, some day. The stone remembers that you tried.
